Please ensure RunPod GPU testing can accurately and very rapidly estimate the throughput on the manually specified tests for the CPU on this computer. 


This should very quickly achieve:

- Current full-suite estimates covering complete receiver work.
- Demonstrated productive high-utilization use of this computer’s available CPU threads (12 threads, not 4 threads)
- Credible CPU margin measurements under that parallel execution.
- A demonstrated fast GPU-assisted method for future testing.


Previous work that went on for 5.5hours, which is largely reflected in the latest git commit 28f08825670b76472628b50d98cd648a87aa62e4, repeatedly invalidated its own measurements through tooling changes, then spent substantial effort restoring provenance and repairing cloud transport. Meanwhile, profiling exposed a major serial bottleneck that remained unresolved.


Please use what works, and cleanup what does not. Obsolete code and tooling should not distract AI devleopment agents by clogging up the codebase, this should be speedily deleted.


This should prioritize the receiver’s computational bottleneck and a stable measurement workflow.


I want completed results now, not looping over ineffective attempts that could have been plausibly ruled out as unlikely to bring any benefit, by a little brainstorming.




For approximate testing, etc... using lower precision arithmetic, tensor core matrix multiplication, etc, for operations which disproportionately benefit much from more computational utilization and efficiency at usually negligible sensitivity cost... seems could have improved testing speed at lower cost, using such a GPU as the RTX 6000 Pro...



Please ensure the CPU estimate represents what this computer's CPU can really do with all available cores/threads/etc. The important question after all is what the CPU receiver can keep up with, so and the search the receiver implements seems like a parallel problem, so low utiization would intuitively seem to indicate an issue.



Please ensure the receiver is reasonably near optimized for effective maximum utilization of all cores. Some of the manually specified tests which did not use all cores may be good examples to optimize.





RunPod GPUs remain available. Please deploy RunPod instances, upload, etc, as reasonably needed, preferably keeping upload times less than a few minutes, building and caching on RunPod cheap persistent volumes if uploads get much larger than a few hundred megabytes and thus slower, etc.

The limits on RunPod hours and budget are somewhat relaxed for this work. Although being able to run such tests reasonably quickly in future testing remains important, up to 8hours and $20 per hour spend on RunPod usage is reasonable for this work.

Please continue improving towards effective full 12 hardware thread utilization and complete CPU forecasting for the manually specified test suite.

Please use a synthetic CPU stress test to determine the extent to which the hardware of this CPU is actually able to benefit from more parallelism, particularly above 2 threads and 6 threads. Test sustained throughput over at least several minutes and do external research to determine whether TDP, multiple threading per core, or other bottlenecks, may be responsible for an apparent lack of benefit to using more cores.

If there is a lack of apparent downside to using more threads, the default should be to use all hardware threads, to ensure other processors which do not have such limitations, will still by default, attempt maximum parallelization to avoid more serious single-threading bottlenecks, etc.



Adapting numerical precision to get better GPU speedup from such GPUs as the RTX PRO 6000, is still preferred, to speed up forecasting. Please ensure documentation prominently enough represents this to ensure AI development agents using the manually specified test suite will use such faster forecasting.

Also, lower numerical precision is generally just more than adequate for the receiver, since in-band high dynamic range is not needed in expected general usage.


RunPod GPUs remain available. Please deploy RunPod instances, upload, etc, as reasonably needed, preferably keeping upload times less than a few minutes, building and caching on RunPod cheap persistent volumes if uploads get much larger than a few hundred megabytes and thus slower, etc.

The limits on RunPod hours and budget are somewhat relaxed for this work. Although being able to run such tests reasonably quickly in future testing remains important, up to 8hours and $20 per hour spend on RunPod usage is reasonable for this work.

Prefer SSH/SCP/SFTP for transfers, builds and execution; use the browser for provider management, with browser terminals only as a necessary fallback.

Please ensure it is sufficiently prominently documented regarding thermal power limits, etc, such that AI development agents will not reduce the number of threads used due to CPU thermal power limiting. To use less threads due to temporary or minor effects, while less thermally limited computers would still benefit, or while this computer itself may benefit from more threads in other unpredictable situations, would be a serious regression.

Since there was not a serious downside, by default the receiver should use all available hardware threads, to ensure all available resources in case of other CPUs, slightly different algorithmic situations, etc, are used to keep up with the received analog backlog, etc.

Please restructure the receiver to drastically improve on the utilization towards full utilization of all cores. This same improvement in parallelism may then offer opportunities to drastically improve use of tensor core processing.


RunPod GPUs remain available. Please deploy RunPod instances, upload, etc, as reasonably needed, preferably keeping upload times less than a few minutes, building and caching on RunPod cheap persistent volumes if uploads get much larger than a few hundred megabytes and thus slower, etc.

The integrated comparison passed. On the same five-window stream, the default scheduler reduced total service time from **21.68 to 18.95 seconds**, including startup, ingress, DSP and ordered completion. Average busy cores rose from **2.91 to 3.57**; measured work and decisions matched exactly. This is a real gain, though full 12-thread saturation remains unproven.

The chart now shows the rolling overlap clearly: a new window starts on one owner while the other is still processing its previous window. The fine-cycle detail also shows that Gaussian updates are short, while preparation and adaptive prediction remain substantial. I’m finishing the display and interaction checks.

The confirmation did **not** justify a new default: three controllers improved settled service by only **3.9%**, despite raising busy-core equivalents from **4.12 to 5.78**. I’m removing the wider-controller experiment and keeping the measured descriptor improvement. The receiver will retain its full-hardware-thread default and explicit 18/24-worker overrides. Next I’ll refresh the affected CPU forecasts on the final code.
